Etymology tree
Proto-Afroasiatic *ʔab-
Proto-Semitic *ʔabw-
Arabic أَبُونَا (ʔabūnā)bor.
Swahili bwanabor.
English bwana
Borrowed from Swahili bwana (“master”), from Arabic أَبُونَا (ʔabūnā, “our father”). Doublet of abbot.
q: It is Jim C.’s custom always to say “Up Simba” in a fake-deep bwana voice as he hefts the camera to his right shoulder […]
2005, David Foster Wallace, Consider the Lobster and Other Essays, New York: Little, Brown and Company, →ISBN, page 208:
Bwahaha, they guffaw as they crush overheads into the corners with the same disdain they display when the clown ahead of them at the airport car-rental counter rents a Hyundai.
2002, Dave Whitehead, The Tennis Junkie's Guide (to Serious Humor), page 41:
“Bwa-ha-ha-ha,” came the unholy mirth from the cold white mask.
